00. Overview & Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate acute vs. chronic low back pain (LBP)
  • Describe the various types of pain and their associated causes
  • Recognize red flag symptoms and their associated conditions
  • Recognize anatomical structures; understand the basic mechanics and forces of the lumbar spine and the pathologies that can lead to LBP
  • Describe dermatomes and myotomes related to back pain
Required reading: Foundations of Osteopathic Medicine, 4th ed., pp. 325–347, 1112–1123, 1292–1295, 1427–1439; Osteopathic Medicine: A Core Concepts Approach, 1st ed., Ch. 5, pp. 59–71. Recommended: An Osteopathic Approach to Diagnosis and Treatment, 4th ed., pp. 241–248.

01. Epidemiology & Burden of Low Back Pain

  • In the U.S., low back pain ranks first among 154 conditions in healthcare spending — about $134.5 billion
  • Global Burden of Disease 2019: LBP is the single leading cause of disability worldwide
  • LBP is the leading cause of years lived with disability (YLDs) worldwide at 63.7 million — compare to diabetes (38.6 million) and COPD (30.6 million)
  • One of the most common reasons for missed work
  • Back pain is the 2nd most common reason for a PCP visit, second only to upper respiratory infection
The good news: acute and subacute LBP has a favorable natural history — in most reported series, the large majority of patients regain function within 6–12 weeks, with or without physician intervention.

02. Acute vs. Subacute vs. Chronic vs. Recurrent LBP

CategoryDurationKey Features
Acute< 6 weeksConnective tissue healing occurs; favorable prognosis — ~60% recover in 6 weeks
Subacute6–12 weeks80–90% recover in 12 weeks
Chronic> 12 weeks (3 months)Often attributed to degenerative or traumatic spinal conditions; connective tissue healing has already occurred; poor prognosis and increased disability — of those disabled >6 months, fewer than half return to work
Recurrence—40–50% of patients have a recurrence within the first 6 months; 70% within 12 months. Most recurrences still carry a favorable prognosis
Practice Question

03. Types of Back Pain

  • Pathology in the back typically causes limitation of movement in the affected spinal region
  • Patients often cannot differentiate whether pain is coming from bone, muscle, joint, or a neighboring structure
  • The reflex reaction to back pain is splinting of the involved segments via muscle spasm — this further blurs the patient's ability to localize the pain
Pain TypeCause / Origin
Radiating painSpinal nerve injury, mediated through the proximal spinal nerves — compression via disc herniation, osteophyte/bone spur, or a space-occupying lesion; leads to local edema, ischemia, and inflammation
Localized painArises from intraspinal structures — blood vessels, dura mater, and the longitudinal ligaments
Non-localized, non-radiating painArises from muscle, bone, and ligament outside the spinal canal
Referred painCan arise from abdominal viscera (aorta, pancreas, duodenum, colon, rectum, kidney, ureter, bladder, pelvic organs) or from systemic illness
Practice Question

04. Differential Diagnosis Categories & Clinical Evaluation

Three categories of LBP

CategoryApprox. frequency
Mechanical low back pain (bone, muscle, ligament)97%
Non-mechanical spinal condition1%
Non-spinal / visceral disease (visceral-somatic)2%

Clinical evaluation — history drives the exam

  • Get a thorough traditional history: location, quality, grade, radiation, history of presenting illness, mechanism of injury
  • Also gather a functional history — current work status and activity level. Key question: "What would you normally be doing that you can't do, or are avoiding, because of this problem?"
  • By the end of the history, you should already have one or several possible diagnoses in mind — the exam exists to explore those possibilities

Three diagnostic questions

  1. Do the presenting symptoms reflect a visceral disorder or a serious/life-threatening illness requiring imaging or further workup? (Screening for red flags)
  2. Where is the pain coming from?
  3. What is happening with this person as a whole that would cause the pain experience to develop and persist? (Biopsychosocial history — dynamic/passive instability, nociceptive system sensitization, psychological factors)

05. Red Flags: The 5 Serious Pathologies

The 5 most common serious pathologies to screen for in acute LBP:

PathologyKey red-flag findings
Vertebral fractureHistory of trauma; history of osteopenia/osteoporosis; history of long-term corticosteroid use
CancerPrevious history of cancer; unable to find a position of relief; fever; unexplained weight loss; blood in stool; pain in multiple sites
InfectionHistory of fever/chills; point tenderness; immunocompromised state; history of diabetes, UTIs, or IV drug use
Cauda equina syndromeBowel or bladder dysfunction (dribbling, inability to start/stop flow); saddle anesthesia (numbness/tingling anywhere that would touch a saddle)
Inflammatory arthritis (the "spondyloarthropathies")Psoriatic arthritis, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis
Practice Question

06. Contraindications to HVLA

These do not necessarily prohibit soft-tissue, low-velocity, or low-amplitude procedures and mobilization — but are important considerations before performing HVLA.

07. Structure/Function Model of LBP Differential Diagnosis

Table 42A.8 from Foundations of Osteopathic Medicine organizes LBP differentials into 5 columns — red flags/spinal pathology, somatic dysfunction (mechanical, OMT-amenable), work-related/behavioral LBP, LBP radiating below the knee (neurological), and inflammatory/metabolic disorders — each broken down by history, physical exam, labs/x-ray, and course.

How to use this table: Somatic dysfunction (mechanical LBP amenable to OMT) classically presents as a well patient with mechanical, activity-dependent pain that does not radiate below the knee, nondiagnostic labs/imaging, and a good prognosis (90% recover from an acute attack in 6 weeks). Contrast this with radiating/neurological LBP (unilateral leg pain greater than back pain, positive reduced SLR, findings limited to one nerve root) or red-flag spinal pathology (age <20 or >55, violent trauma, constant progressive nonmechanical pain, systemic symptoms).
Practice Question

09. Bones, Ligaments & Vertebral Anatomy

  • 5 lumbar vertebrae, progressively enlarging from L1 to L5 — this helps transmit and support the load of the head, thorax, and upper extremities down the spine
  • Resists anterior gravitational movement by maintaining lumbar lordosis

Key structures

  • Superior + inferior articular processes combine to form the zygapophyseal (facet) joint — a common source of mechanical LBP
  • Facet joints in the upper lumbar spine lie more in the sagittal plane (favoring flexion/extension); further down the lumbar spine (toward L5–S1) they shift toward a more oblique/coronal plane (favoring side-bending and rotation)
  • Pars interarticularis ("isthmus"/"island of bone") — the bone between the superior and inferior articular processes. Under chronic traumatic stress it can fracture, producing the classic "Scotty dog" fracture on oblique X-ray (fracture line at the "collar" of the dog) — think spondylolisthesis
  • Intervertebral foramen — the space nerve roots exit through. Its size is dictated by disc height and pedicle shape. As discs lose height with degeneration, the posterior longitudinal ligament may hypertrophy and osteophytes/bone spurs may form — all of which narrow the foramen and can produce nerve root ("pinched nerve") symptoms

Ligaments

TypeExamplesNotes
Multisegmental (span multiple levels)Anterior longitudinal ligament, posterior longitudinal ligament—
Segmental (span one level)Interspinous, supraspinous, intertransverse ligamentsSupraspinous ligament provides the most resistance to flexion (connects tips of spinous processes); interspinous ligament runs oblique to the spine's compressive axis — functionally similar to knee collateral ligaments, helping guide flexion while limiting transverse/frontal motion

10. Muscles of the Back & Trunk

These muscles provide stability to the spine during dynamic movements and actions:

  • Latissimus dorsi
  • Erector spinae (iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis)
  • Rotatores, multifidi
  • Internal obliques, transversus abdominis
  • Gluteus maximus, medius, minimus
  • Psoas, iliacus
  • Quadratus lumborum
  • Piriformis

11. Spinal Motion & Segmental Mobility

  • Spinal motion is the combination of the intervertebral joints and the facet joints
  • Reportedly 15–40% of LBP stems from the facet joints
  • Facet joints guide intervertebral motion through their plane orientation (frontal/sagittal/coronal) and help protect the disc from excessive twisting or hyperflexion, and help resist excessive rotation

Segmental mobility depends on:

  1. Vertebral body/disc size — disc height maintains alignment of joint surfaces and tension on the segmental supporting ligaments
  2. Facet orientation — sagittal plane (upper lumbar) favors flexion/extension; as the plane becomes more frontal/coronal (lower lumbar), more rotation and side-bending are allowed. Disc-space narrowing from degeneration changes the positional relationship of vertebrae to one another, adversely affecting joint mechanics

12. The Intervertebral Disc

  • Along with the bones, provides static stability
  • The largest avascular structure in the body

Annulus fibrosus

  • Composed of 10–20 layers of fibrocartilaginous fibers that insert onto the vertebral body
  • Houses nociceptors and proprioceptive nerve endings

Nucleus pulposus

  • Gelatinous mucopolysaccharide center, ~90% water — this water content decreases with age
  • Composed of a protein-bound chondroitin sulfate (proteoglycan) that gives the disc its hydrophilic/fluid-maintaining capacity
  • Provides extra strength during compression
  • Nutrition depends on diffusion of water — only the outer third of the disc has a blood supply
Aging pearl: As the disc dehydrates/degenerates, it loses its ability to develop internal fluid pressure and transform compressive loads into radial (hoop) force on the annulus fibrosus. This shifts more load onto the vertebral bodies themselves, driving further degenerative changes (osteophyte/bone spur formation) — i.e., degenerative disc disease leads to degenerative joint disease.

13. Innervation of the Lumbar Spine & Disc Herniation

Plexuses

PlexusRoot LevelsKey Nerves
Lumbar plexusL1–L4 (+T12); passes through psoas majorIliohypogastric, ilioinguinal, genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, obturator, femoral, + short direct muscular branches
Sacral plexusL4–S4; lies between piriformis and pelvic fasciaSciatic (common fibular + tibial divisions), superior & inferior gluteal, posterior cutaneous femoral, nerves to quadratus femoris/obturator internus/piriformis
Pudendal & coccygeal plexusS2–S4, S5–Co1Pudendal, perineal, dorsal nerve of penis/clitoris, anococcygeal
Remember: the spinal cord itself ends around L1–L2 (conus medullaris), but nerve roots continue down within the dural sac as the cauda equina.

Nerve roots & disc herniation

  • Nerve roots exit above the disc, through the foraminal opening
  • An L3 disc herniation affects the L4 nerve root (or below)
  • An L4 disc herniation affects the L5 nerve root (or below)
  • An L5 disc herniation affects the S1 nerve root (or below)
  • The most common disc herniations occur at L4–L5 and L5–S1
Practice Question

15. Facet Joint Dysfunction

  • Facet joints are lined with smooth cartilage and lubricated with synovial fluid
  • They guide intervertebral motion through their orientation in the transverse and frontal planes, and limit motion to protect the disc from excessive twisting/hyperflexion
  • These joints react to trauma and inflammation — producing pain, stiffness, and dysfunction, with secondary muscle spasm leading to further joint stiffness and degeneration
  • Reportedly 15–40% of LBP stems from facet joint involvement

16. Types of Segmental Loading & Forces

Four main types of segmental loading on the lumbar spine: axial compression, bending (flexion/extension), torsion (rotation), and shear (side-bending stresses are considered together with rotational stress in the summary below).

Axial compression

  • Caused by gravity, ground reaction forces, muscle contraction, or ligament reactions to tensile forces
  • Hoop stress: the disc tolerates compressive load by converting vertically applied compression into circumferentially applied tension
  • As compressive load increases pressure within the nucleus pulposus, that pressure is exerted radially against the surrounding annulus fibrosus
  • Most load is carried anteriorly (the thickest portion of the disc); the posterior disc can carry 0–30% of the load depending on segment/position — this is why most disc herniations are posterior or posterolateral (the weaker portion)

Bending (flexion and extension)

  • A combination of compression, shear, and tensile forces on the segment from translation
  • The nucleus pulposus tends to deform in the direction opposite the applied load
  • Flexion: NP deforms posteriorly; superior vertebra anteriorly tilts/forward glides; intervertebral foramen widens ~24%; anterior compression, posterior tension (posterior longitudinal ligament + supraspinous ligament); central canal widens. Segments are recruited superior-to-inferior (upper lumbar moves first)
  • Extension: NP deforms anteriorly; posterior disc sustains compressive force, anterior segment undergoes tensile loading; superior vertebra tilts/glides posteriorly; intervertebral foramen narrows ~20%; central canal narrows. Overall lumbar extension range is much less than flexion due to lumbar bony geometry (spinous processes approximate one another; anterior longitudinal ligament tension restricts motion)

Torsion

  • Caused by axial rotation and coupled motion
  • The disc is much less tolerant of torsional/rotational forces — annulus fibrosus fibers run obliquely, so during rotation only a portion of the fibers are under tension at any given time (limiting the disc's ability to resist torsional stress)
  • Facet joints help limit rotation and protect against these forces
  • When torsion is combined with flexion, the force required for tissue failure decreases significantly (classic mechanism: bending, lifting, and twisting — e.g., shoveling snow — is when the disc is most vulnerable)
Practice Question

17. Summary of Forces: Tissues & Injuries

ForceTissues ResistingTypical Injury
Compressive (axial) loadingVertebral bodies, intervertebral disc, abdominal mechanismVertebral body or endplate fracture
Rotational & side-bending stressFacet joints, pedicles, abdominal mechanism, quadratus lumborum, superficial & deep back musclesFracture of the pars interarticularis or pedicle
Flexion stressPosterior ligament system, posterior annulus fibrosus, thoracodorsal fascia, superficial & deep back musclesAnnular tear, disc herniation, muscle injury
Extension stressAnterior ligament system, posterior bony elements, abdominal mechanismPars fracture, traumatic spondylolisthesis
Protection of neurovascular elementsFibro-osseous foramina (intervertebral foramina)Entrapment of cauda equina and/or nerve roots

19. Non-Mechanical Spinal Causes of LBP

Recall the 3 diagnostic categories of LBP: mechanical (~97%), non-mechanical spinal (~1%), and non-spinal/visceral (~2%). This section covers the non-mechanical spinal causes.

Neoplasm — bony metastases

  • Metastasize directly to spine: breast, lung, prostate (marked with * as most notable), also adrenal, colon, thyroid, kidney
  • Prostate cancer pearl: new LBP can be the presenting sign of metastatic prostate cancer — this should prompt an immediate digital rectal exam (and consideration of PSA, imaging) if a prostatic mass is felt

Inflammatory arthritis

  • Ankylosing spondylitis
  • Psoriatic (spondylitis) arthritis
  • Reactive arthritis (Reiter's syndrome)
  • Rheumatoid arthritis
  • Spinal arachnoiditis
  • Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis (pain can radiate to the spine)

Disorders affecting the spine

DisorderKey features
Paget's diseaseMainly affects those of Northern European descent, age >50; bone remodeling is disrupted, causing bones to become fragile and misshapen; treated (not cured) with bisphosphonates
Scheuermann disease (osteochondrosis, aka juvenile kyphosis)Vertebrae in children form a wedge shape, leading to painful kyphosis; treated with bracing and a supervised exercise program to allow correct bone remodeling
DISH (diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis)Soft tissues (ligaments, tendons, fascia around joints) stiffen and calcify; treated with exercise and pain relief

Infection

  • Osteomyelitis
  • Septic discitis
  • Paraspinous abscess
  • Spinal epidural abscess
  • Meningitis
  • Spinal arachnoiditis
None of these non-mechanical spinal conditions are typically candidates for OMT as primary treatment — the exception is once the patient is undergoing appropriate treatment and needs adjunctive care to improve the efficiency of healing.

20. Visceral (Referred) Causes of Back Pain

SystemConditions
CardiorespiratoryPericarditis, pleurisy/pleuritic disease, pneumonia
Pelvic organsProstatitis, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), endometriosis
RenalNephrolithiasis (kidney stones), pyelonephritis, perinephric abscess
VascularAbdominal or thoracic aortic aneurysm — causes back pain because of its direct proximity to the spine
GastrointestinalPancreatitis, pancreatic cancer, cholecystitis/gallstones, peptic ulcers
DermatologicShingles (herpes zoster) — unilateral, dermatomal back pain; pain can precede the rash, so early treatment is important once suspected
Key concept: visceral-somatic reflexes can cause back pain, and the exact region of back pain can sometimes help narrow the visceral differential — this is the same reflex arc concept underlying Chapman's points.

22. Bone & Ligament Dysfunctions

  • Fractures (acute or chronic) need proper workup to determine whether casting/splinting or surgery is needed
  • Somatic dysfunction — often something you can address quickly, giving the patient immediate relief without a long workup
  • Scoliosis / structural short leg — not curable with OMT, but quality of life can be improved by addressing pain from the body's compensation for the underlying structural issue
  • Inflammatory arthritis — treatment approach depends on location and whether the patient is in a flare; even in non-acute periods, gentle techniques are preferred if OMT is used

Ligament sprains

Typically occur with:

  • Sudden, violent muscle contraction
  • Sudden torsion/twisting motion
  • Severe direct blows
  • Forceful straightening from a crouched position (especially with twisting involved)
Posterior ligaments are more prone to injury than anterior ligaments.

23. Spondylosis, Spondylolysis & Spondylolisthesis

These three terms are easy to confuse — each refers to a different level of damage to a vertebral segment and/or disc:

TermDefinition
SpondylosisDegenerative changes within the intervertebral disc and adjacent vertebral bodies/joints (this is the end result of degenerative disc disease — see next section)
SpondylolysisA defect/fracture in the pars interarticularis, without anterior displacement of the vertebral body
SpondylolisthesisAnterior displacement of one vertebra relative to the one below — usually occurs because of a pars interarticularis fracture (spondylolysis)
Epidemiology pearl: spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis are the most common causes of back pain in children older than 10 years.

The "Scotty dog" sign

On a 45° oblique X-ray view of the lumbar spine, the posterior elements of a vertebra resemble a Scotty dog:

Scotty dog partAnatomic structure
EyePedicle
EarSuperior articular process
NoseTransverse process
NeckPars interarticularis
BodyLamina
TailSpinous process
Front legInferior articular process
Hind legContralateral inferior articular process
If the pars interarticularis (the "neck") is fractured, the dog appears to be wearing a collar — this is spondylolysis. If the vertebra then slips forward, the dog appears to be decapitated — this is spondylolisthesis.
Practice Question

24. Degenerative Disc Disease & Facet Arthropathy

Pathophysiology

  • Begins with changes in the intervertebral discs, eventually affecting the facet joints and vertebrae
  • Primary causes: genetics, aging, lifestyle — especially smoking (impairs collagen maintenance) and obesity (increases disc pressure)
  • Over time, annulus fibrosus collagen changes and becomes more susceptible to tears/fissures
  • Discogenic pain arises only from the outer third of the annulus (where innervation exists) — tears in the inner two-thirds don't directly cause pain
  • Water-attracting proteoglycans in the nucleus pulposus decrease → the disc dehydrates, reducing its ability to handle motion, torsion, shear, and compression
  • Disc space decreases → irritation of facet joints → hypermobility and segmental instability → vertebrae rub together → osteophyte formation to stabilize the spine = spondylosis

Who gets it?

  • Young to middle-aged persons, peak incidence around age 40; affects all genders equally
  • Prevalence increases with age, but degenerated discs are not necessarily painful — imaging shows DDD about equally in symptomatic and asymptomatic people

Discogenic pain — clinical pattern

  • Onset: traumatic (bending + twisting) or spontaneous; pain usually aching, sometimes sore/stabbing especially at onset
  • Worse in the morning (sudden pressure increase on the disc with standing)
  • Relieved by: side-lying/fetal-like position, changing position, or becoming more active
  • Aggravated by: prolonged sitting, standing up from sitting, forward flexion, lifting, coughing/sneezing/laughing/Valsalva, vibration (car, train)

Facet arthropathy — clinical pattern

Similar aggravating factors to discogenic pain (prolonged sitting/standing, vibration) except: facet pain is worse with extension (which closes/loads the facet joints) and relieved with flexion (which takes pressure off the facets).

Practice Question

25. Disc Bulge & Herniation

  • Bulging vs. herniated discs — whether there is nerve root impingement depends on the position of the bulge/herniation
  • 25–60% of disc herniations are asymptomatic
  • Most common pattern: posterolateral herniation
  • L4–L5 and L5–S1 account for ~95% of all herniations

Clinical signs suggesting disc herniation

  • Pain aggravated by flexion (pushes vertebral bodies/discs closer together posteriorly)
  • Positive straight leg raise (Lasègue) test
  • Radicular signs/symptoms corresponding to the position of the suspected herniation

26. Joint Dysfunctions: SI, Hip & Femoroacetabular

In addition to the disc and facet joints, low back pain can be referred from or caused by the sacroiliac and femoroacetabular (hip) joints. All of these joints react to trauma, including repetitive microtrauma, leading to inflammation → pain, stiffness, and dysfunction with secondary muscle spasm → further joint stiffness and degeneration.

Sacroiliitis

  • Inflammation of one or both SI joints
  • History: pain in the buttocks and lower back, may radiate down one or both legs; worse with prolonged standing or climbing stairs
  • Causes: trauma, osteoarthritis, inflammatory arthritis (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis), pregnancy, infection

27. Cauda Equina & Peripheral Nerve Anatomy

Central: conus medullaris & cauda equina

  • The spinal cord is a solid structure until it reaches the conus medullaris, around L1–L2
  • Below that, it spreads into the cauda equina ("horse's tail") — nerve root pairs L2–L5, S1–S5, and the coccygeal nerve
  • The cauda equina innervates the pelvic organs, provides motor innervation to the lower limbs and the internal/external anal sphincters, sensory innervation to the perineum, and partial parasympathetic innervation to the bladder
This is exactly why cauda equina syndrome produces its classic red flags: saddle anesthesia (perineal sensory loss), bowel/bladder dysfunction (motor + parasympathetic bladder involvement), and lower-limb motor/sensory deficits — all from one compressive lesion at this level.

Peripheral: lumbar spinal nerves

  • Anterior rami communicate with the sympathetic trunk, pass behind psoas major, and form the lumbar and sacral plexuses
  • Posterior rami supply the erector spinae muscles and the skin of the back
A reminder from the lecturer: recognizing cauda equina syndrome early matters — missing it can permanently affect a patient's quality of life. This point was made personally, noting a family member's diagnosis came too late.

28. Lumbar Radiculopathy: Level-by-Level Findings

  • Radiculopathy = burning/shooting ("electric") pain radiating into a unilateral lower extremity in a dermatomal distribution
  • Compression impairs nerve function → sensory changes and/or motor weakness
  • Deep tendon reflexes corresponding to the affected root are often diminished
  • Key rule: a disc herniation affects the lower nerve root — an L4–L5 disc herniation causes L5 radiculopathy; an L5–S1 disc herniation causes S1 radiculopathy

Quick summary by level

  • L1 — rare; inguinal region pain/paresthesia; no motor weakness; normal reflexes
  • L2 — anterolateral-to-medial upper thigh pain/sensory loss; hip flexion weakness; normal reflexes
  • L3 — distal anterior/medial thigh to knee; hip flexion, adduction, knee extension weakness; diminished patellar reflex
  • L4 — lateral-to-anterior thigh to anterior leg; medial lower leg/ankle/foot sensory loss; knee extension + ankle dorsiflexion weakness; screening test = squat and rise; diminished/absent patellar reflex
  • L5 — most common radiculopathy, classically causes foot drop; posterolateral thigh/lower leg/dorsal foot pain; numbness at the 1st web space and dorsal foot; weakness in ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension, foot inversion/eversion, hip abduction; screening test = heel walk; normal or diminished internal hamstring reflex (this one doesn't always follow the usual pattern)
  • S1 — posterior thigh/calf/heel pain; lateral ankle/heel/toes/sole numbness; weakness in ankle/toe plantarflexion and hip extension; screening test = toe walk; diminished/absent Achilles reflex
Radiculopathy is present in 3–5% of LBP cases, with L5 the most common. Causes: disc herniation, spondylolisthesis, or spinal stenosis.
Practice Questions

29. Spinal Stenosis

  • Narrowing of the spinal canal — central, lateral, and/or neuroforaminal stenosis
  • Most common in adults >60 years old
  • History: back pain, frequently with radiculopathy that is unrelated to activity
  • Neurogenic claudication: burning pain ± numbness in the low back, buttocks, or lower extremities — aggravated by walking or standing, relieved by sitting and lumbar flexion
  • May involve gait changes, lower-extremity weakness, sensory loss, or fatigue/decreased stamina (from the extra energy needed to compensate)

30. Cauda Equina Syndrome

  • Caused by serious impingement of the cauda equina or spinal cord in the upper lumbar region — from disc herniation (HNP), severe spinal stenosis, infection, or trauma (e.g., epidural hematoma after a fall)
  • Rare but severe — a surgical emergency
  • Can present with or without prior LBP history; can be acute or gradual in onset

Clinical presentation

  • Low back pain
  • Changes in bladder/bowel function; loss of sphincter control (retention or incontinence)
  • Sexual dysfunction
  • Unilateral or bilateral radiculopathy involving one or multiple nerve roots
  • Saddle anesthesia
  • Reflex changes: DTRs, bulbocavernosus and/or cremasteric reflexes
Don't miss this — be especially careful in patients with a flat affect (e.g., Parkinson's disease, autism, or other conditions affecting typical symptom reporting), since they may not communicate these red-flag symptoms in a typical way.
Practice Question

31. Muscular Causes of LBP

  • Iliopsoas syndrome — common in people who sit a lot (e.g., medical students!) and then stand suddenly; patients often report they "can't stand up straight" without pain
  • Piriformis syndrome — common in those who sit with a thick wallet or an uneven cushion that skews the pelvis; pain in one buttock ± radiation down the posterior/lateral thigh, making it hard to find a comfortable seated position. There is a notable correlation between increased stress and piriformis flare-ups
  • Muscle hypertonicity/imbalance — one muscle tight, its antagonist loose; spasm often occurs when one muscle compensates by doing both its own job and that of its ipsilateral synergist
  • Strains/sprains that don't cause disc herniation or bulge can still lead to tendinitis or bursitis
Histories for muscular causes vary widely from person to person, even with the same underlying problem.

32. History & Pattern Recognition

HistoryInitial Hypothesis
Restricted lumbar motion with low back/buttock pain exacerbated by a specific movement pattern suggesting opening or closing joint restriction (e.g., decreased extension + right sidebending + right rotation)Zygapophyseal (facet) joint pain syndrome
Centralization or peripheralization of symptoms during repetitive movement or prolonged positioningPossible discogenic pain
Lower extremity pain/paresthesia worse than the LBP itself; possible episodes of LE weaknessPossible sciatica or lumbar radiculopathy
LE pain exacerbated by extension, quickly relieved by flexionPossible spinal stenosis
Recurrent locking, catching, or "giving way" of the low back during active motionPossible lumbar instability
LBP exacerbated by stretching of ligaments/muscles, or pain with muscular contractionMuscle/ligamentous sprain or strain

33. Physical Exam & Special Tests

Inspection / observation

  • Deformity? Change in normal spinal curves (hyperlordosis, flattened lordosis, excessive kyphosis, scoliosis)?
  • Preferred patient positioning — seated? standing? pacing?

Palpation

  • Tenderness to palpation — where? Does it reproduce symptoms?

Range of motion (active & passive)

  • Pain with flexion is common in general
  • Deviation to one side with forward flexion may indicate a posterolateral disc bulge on the opposite side
  • Extension tends to alleviate discogenic pain but irritate inflammation
  • Localized unilateral paralumbar pain with extension may indicate facet syndrome
  • Restricted flexion may suggest an inflammatory spondyloarthropathy

Special tests

TestWhat it tells you
Straight leg raise (SLR / Lasègue)Reproduces radicular pain with leg elevation
Contralateral / crossed SLRPain occurs when raising the opposite leg — more specific for lumbar radiculopathy than the standard SLR
FABERE (Patrick's test)Anterior/groin pain suggests intrinsic hip dysfunction; posterior/SI-region pain suggests SI joint dysfunction
Pelvic rockingDiscogenic stress maneuver — flex the patient's hips until the knees approximate the chest, then rotate the lower extremities side to side; reproduces discogenic pain
Sustained hip flexionSupine, raise extended LEs to 60°, have the patient hold and then release; assess for low back/buttock pain, then repeat at 15° — pain that increases as the legs lower is a positive test
On the osteopathic structural exam, somatic dysfunction related to LBP is most often found in the lumbar spine, pelvis, sacrum, lower extremities, and lower thoracic spine.

35. Imaging & Special Testing Decision Guide

StudyIndications
Plain X-rayNot recommended for routine evaluation of acute LBP without red flags. Recommended to rule out fracture. Oblique views only when spondylolysis/spondylolisthesis is suspected
MRI or CT myelographyBack-related leg symptoms with clinically detectable nerve root compromise; history of neurogenic claudication suspicious for spinal stenosis; findings suggesting cauda equina syndrome, fracture, infection, or tumor
Bone scanSuspected occult fracture (especially pars interarticularis stress fracture) or suspected metastatic disease. Contraindicated in pregnancy (uses radioactive tracer)
Electrophysiologic tests (EMG, SPEP)Questionable nerve root dysfunction with leg symptoms >6 weeks and an unclear picture. Not needed if radiculopathy is already obviously explained by known disc disease
Practical note: a patient with an intrinsic tremor undergoing MRI may need to be sedated for the study, or motion artifact can make the images equivocal or unusable.

36. Role of OMT & General Treatment Principles

OMT in red-flag cases

  • OMT is not first-line treatment when red flags are present — get the appropriate workup and identify the underlying problem first
  • OMT can add value once the patient is stabilized and sinister pathology has been excluded/is being actively managed — helping reduce pain, facilitate healing (via lymphatic flow), and address somatic dysfunction that interferes with the body's own healing capacity
  • If using OMT, gentle, indirect techniques for shorter duration are more appropriate
  • Therapeutic touch also has real psychological value — maintaining physical contact and eye contact, or simply sitting with a patient, can be meaningfully healing

General management (mechanical LBP, >95% of cases)

  • Acute phase: focus on pain control and gradually improving function; keep the patient as active as possible while awaiting spontaneous recovery
  • Activity modification: limit/avoid aggravating positions or activities that increase mechanical stress (prolonged unsupported sitting, heavy lifting, bending/twisting)
  • Bed rest: generally NOT recommended, except short duration (usually <4 days) for severe initial symptoms when the patient truly cannot get out of bed
  • Medications: oral vs. injectable (epidural or facet injections) vs. topical, usually only needed short-term. Steroids (oral or injectable) may be considered for chronic conditions — use caution in patients with diabetes, since systemic steroids can temporarily worsen glucose control
  • OMT: gentle/indirect techniques tend to suit acute pain better; chronic pain often responds well to more direct techniques
  • Physical agents/modalities: heat, ice, TENS, shoe inserts, bracing, acupuncture
  • Exercise: focus on strengthening/stabilizing the core and spine, and stretching the hip flexors — this also helps reduce fear-avoidance behavior and supports function despite ongoing pain
  • Consider referral to PT/OT as needed, and remember to treat the whole patient — body, mind, and soul, since trauma can cause more than just physical problems

Scotty dog "collar"= spondylolysis (pars interarticularis fracture)
Scotty dog "decapitated"= spondylolisthesis (vertebral slip)

Most common herniation levelsL4–L5 and L5–S1 (~95% of all herniations); posterolateral most common location
Radiculopathy prevalence3–5% of LBP; L5 radiculopathy most common (classic "foot drop")
Reflex by levelL3/L4 → patellar; L5 → internal hamstring (atypical); S1 → Achilles
Spinal stenosis hallmarkNeurogenic claudication — worse with walking/standing, relieved with sitting/flexion; age >60
Cauda equina syndromeRare, surgical emergency; saddle anesthesia + bowel/bladder dysfunction + sexual dysfunction; caused by HNP, severe stenosis, infection, or trauma
Crossed/contralateral SLRMore specific than standard SLR for lumbar radiculopathy
FABERE testGroin pain = hip; posterior/SI pain = SI joint dysfunction
